summary_markdown: # Indiana — Commercial UAS Regulatory Summary **Prepared for:** AEC (surveying, mapping, construction, inspection) UAS program management **Research date:** August 1, 2026 | **Version:** 2.2 (Workstream 9 retrofit — August 7, 2026) **Model / checkpoint:** Claude Sonnet 5 (research and drafting); retrofit pass also performed with claude-sonnet-5. **Interpretation scope:** Agent Instructions v6 (August 2, 2026) **Scope note:** Federal FAA Part 107 is the baseline for all commercial sUAS operations nationwide and is not restated here. Per current research-phase scope (Agent Instructions v6, Amendment 2), this summary covers Indiana **state and state-agency** UAS authorities only — municipal and county ordinances are deferred. Unlike some states in this program (e.g., Illinois), **no statewide statute preempting local UAS ordinances was located for Indiana**; at least two Indiana cities (Fort Wayne and Carmel) maintain their own drone ordinances, which is inconsistent with a preemption regime being in force. Full citations and metadata are in `IN_UAS_Source_Register.csv`. > **Status:** A first pass of source collection, objective summaries, and practical interpretation is complete for this state. Ongoing work is expanding source coverage and improving quality review and processing efficiency across the project. --- ## 1. State UAS Regulatory Overview Indiana regulates UAS through a cluster of targeted criminal statutes rather than one omnibus drone act, several of which are private-operator-facing and already in force — a notable contrast with states whose comparable provisions remain only proposed. IC 35-33-5-9 requires a search warrant before a law-enforcement officer may use a UAV on or over private property or to surveil it. Separately, Indiana's Title 35 contains three private-operator-facing UAV offenses: remote aerial voyeurism (IC 35-45-4-5(g)-(h)), remote aerial harassment (IC 35-45-10-6) — recently and substantially expanded, effective July 1, 2026, to reach drone-based harassment of livestock, crop damage, and interference with farm operations after a wave of farmer complaints tied to avian-flu fears — and public safety remote aerial interference (IC 35-44.1-4-10), which bars using a UAV to obstruct law enforcement, fire, EMS, or search-and-rescue personnel. Indiana's 2024 Senate Enrolled Act 182 added UAV-specific contraband-trafficking offenses at correctional facilities (IC 35-44.1-3-5, -3-6), and a long-standing wildlife statute (IC 14-22-6-16) bars using a UAV to scout game during a defined pre-season/season window, subject to an agricultural-monitoring exception — a statute now under its first-ever prosecution (2026). On state land, Indiana DNR's administrative rule (312 IAC 8-2-8(i)) is an unqualified prohibition on UAV landing/launch on DNR property, though DNR's own guidance describes a discretionary licensing practice outside the rule's text. A new counter-UAS statute (IC 10-22, 2026) designates the Indiana State Police as the statewide coordinating agency for federally-authorized detection and mitigation activity near critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, and airports, though its substantive authority remains contingent on a federal trigger that had not been confirmed as satisfied as of this research date. Governor Braun's Executive Order 25-73 (October 2025) created a state drone-industry task force, not an operator-facing rule. No statewide preemption of local UAS ordinances, no UAS-specific Attorney General opinion or court decision, and no general state-agency foreign-manufacturer procurement restriction (of the kind Illinois' IDOT has adopted) were located. ## 2. Statewide UAS Laws and Regulations ### Unmanned Aerial Vehicles; Search Warrant; Exceptions — IC 35-33-5-9 *Binding law | Current, originally P.L.170-2014, most recently amended by P.L.136-2019* **Objective Summary:** Requires a law enforcement officer to obtain a search warrant to use a UAV (1) on or over private property, or (2) to search, surveil, photograph, or video private property or persons/items/structures on private property, without the affected owner's consent. A warrant is not required if one would not be required for the same search conducted without a UAV. This statute governs law-enforcement conduct only; it does not directly regulate private/commercial UAS operators. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Design acquisition and data-handling workflows to minimize unnecessary capture of people and private activity. Confirm the source-supported consent or project-purpose basis before flight and carry that limitation through processing, access control, retention, and delivery. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Document the applicability analysis and any exception relied upon in the project file. Align the scope, client representations, and operator procedures with the verified authority, and seek state counsel if material facts fall outside its clear terms. ### Remote Aerial Voyeurism — IC 35-45-4-5(g)-(h) *Binding law | Current, remote-aerial-voyeurism subsections added by P.L.107-2017* **Objective Summary:** Makes it a Class A misdemeanor (Level 6 felony for a repeat offense, or if the material is published, posted online, or transmitted to another person) for a person, with intent to peep, to operate a UAV so that it enters the airspace above or surrounding another person's occupied dwelling to capture images, photographs, video, or audio of that person while inside the dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area, without consent. This is a subsection of Indiana's broader voyeurism statute and is distinct from the separate remote aerial harassment offense below. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Do not operate a UAV with intent to peep or capture images of a person inside an occupied dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area, without consent — this is a felony-eligible offense distinct from the broader voyeurism statute. Routine AEC survey, inspection, and mapping photography is not the conduct this subsection targets, but frame flight paths and camera angles to avoid incidental capture into private dwelling interiors, and never publish, post, or transmit any such incidental capture given subsection (h)'s felony-elevation trigger for publication. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Treat the cited authority as a documented compliance gate where applicable. Preserve the facts supporting any exception or consent theory, allocate client and operator responsibilities clearly, and seek state counsel when project facts approach ambiguous or penal language. ### Remote Aerial Harassment — IC 35-45-10-6 *Binding law | Current, originally P.L.107-2017; substantively amended by H.E.A. 1249 (P.L.158-2026), eff. July 1, 2026* **Objective Summary:** As currently codified in the primary-source mirrors reviewed, this statute makes it remote aerial harassment, a Class A misdemeanor (Level 6 felony on repeat offense), to operate a UAV in a manner intended to subject another person to harassment. Multiple independent news outlets report that House Enrolled Act 1249 (P.L.158-2026), effective July 1, 2026, expanded the offense so that operating a drone over another's property with intent to harass or disturb livestock, damage crops, or interfere with agricultural operations is also a Class A misdemeanor. **Citation currency flag (reconfirmed in this retrofit pass):** as of August 7, 2026 — more than five weeks after the amendment's effective date — the Justia and FindLaw codification mirrors still display only the pre-amendment single-sentence version; the amended text itself has still not been independently verified against a primary codified source across two research passes. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Do not operate a UAV in a manner intended to harass another person, or — once the July 1, 2026 livestock/crops/farm-operations amendment takes effect in the codified text — to harass or disturb livestock, damage crops, or interfere with farm operations. Obtain the landowner's documented permission before any agricultural, corridor, or rural-property flight, and brief crews that intent to harass (not merely proximity to livestock or crops) is the operative element, consistent with the law's stated goal of preserving legitimate agricultural drone uses such as crop monitoring and chemical application. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Treat the cited authority as a documented compliance gate where applicable. Preserve the facts supporting any exception or consent theory, allocate client and operator responsibilities clearly, and seek state counsel when project facts approach ambiguous or penal language. ### Trafficking With an Inmate / Trafficking With an Inmate Outside a Facility (UAV-delivered contraband) — IC 35-44.1-3-5, IC 35-44.1-3-6 *Binding law | Current, amended 2024 by P.L.22-2024 (Senate Enrolled Act 182, signed March 11, 2024)* **Objective Summary:** Makes it trafficking with an inmate, a Class A misdemeanor (Level 5 felony for certain contraband), to deliver, carry, or receive an article to or from an inmate or juvenile-facility resident without the facility head's prior authorization, expressly including delivery, carrying, or receipt "through the use of an unmanned aerial vehicle" (Sec. 5). A parallel offense (Sec. 6) covers delivering or placing contraband by UAV for an inmate being transported outside a facility. Both sections were amended in 2024 after the Indiana Department of Correction reported more than 30 drone sightings and over a dozen confirmed drone-delivered contraband drops at state correctional facilities in 2023. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Secure the facility head's prior written authorization before any UAV flight at or near a correctional or juvenile facility, regardless of the flight's purpose — the statute's prior-authorization requirement is the only avoidance mechanism and applies to any person, not just inmates or visitors. Confirm the facility's specific point of contact, required lead time, and any site-specific conditions well before mobilization. - **Agency Practitioner:** Contact the protected facility's owner, operator, administrator, commander, or other official identified by the authority before mobilization and ask whether the proposed AEC mission qualifies for written approval or an employment/contractor exception. Provide the site, purpose, dates, flight area, crew and aircraft details the facility requests, and retain the signed authorization and security conditions; do not assume ordinary site access or a client work order is sufficient. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Make the required approval and compliance with its conditions a documented mobilization gate. Allocate responsibility for applications and schedule impacts in the contract, and obtain counsel if the project's facts do not fit the stated authorization pathway. ### Public Safety Remote Aerial Interference — IC 35-44.1-4-10 *Binding law | Current, originally P.L.107-2017, amended by P.L.22-2024* **Objective Summary:** Makes it a Class A misdemeanor (Level 6 felony on repeat offense) to operate a UAV in a manner intended to obstruct or interfere with a law enforcement officer (including a correctional officer), a firefighter, an emergency medical person, or a member of a search-and-rescue team or mission, while that individual is performing official duties. The 2024 amendment added correctional officers to the list of covered officials. This is a private-operator-facing offense already in force in Indiana, distinct from and broader than the law-enforcement-only search-warrant statute above. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Screen the project map for protected facilities and active emergency operations before dispatch. Establish conservative stand-off and escalation points, brief the crew on the applicable restriction, and document any source-supported authorization before entering the affected area. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Treat the cited authority as a documented compliance gate where applicable. Preserve the facts supporting any exception or consent theory, allocate client and operator responsibilities clearly, and seek state counsel when project facts approach ambiguous or penal language. ### Use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles to Aid Hunting — IC 14-22-6-16 *Binding law | Current, originally P.L.111-2016, most recently amended by P.L.25-2024* **Objective Summary:** Prohibits knowingly using a UAV to search for, scout, locate, or detect a wild animal covered by a hunting season, as an aid to taking it, during a window beginning 14 days before that season and ending at the close of legal hunting hours on the season's last day. UAV use with infrared capability to locate and recover an already-legally-taken animal is expressly permitted, but does not authorize entering another's property without permission. Exceptions cover DNR and its designees, government agents performing official duties, educational/research institution personnel for bona fide purposes, veterinary care of a specific wild animal, and monitoring of agricultural production or nuisance wild animals. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Plan environmental and mapping flights to avoid conduct that could be characterized as locating, pursuing, disturbing, or harassing wildlife. Coordinate mission timing and stand-off distances with the land manager when project work overlaps sensitive habitat or hunting activity. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Document the applicability analysis and any exception relied upon in the project file. Align the scope, client representations, and operator procedures with the verified authority, and seek state counsel if material facts fall outside its clear terms. ## 3. State Agency and Facility-Specific UAS Requirements ### Indiana Department of Natural Resources — Airborne-Device Prohibition on DNR Property (312 IAC 8-2-8(i)) *Binding administrative regulation | Current, most recently amended/readopted 2024; exception practice RESOLVED in this retrofit pass* **Objective Summary:** Prohibits a person from landing, taxiing, taking off, parking, or mooring an unmanned motor-driven airborne device (or an airborne human transportation device) on DNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property — including state parks, state forests, state recreation areas, nature preserves, fish and wildlife areas, and reservoir properties — except at a site the Department has designated for that purpose. The rule's own text contains no enumerated exceptions. This retrofit pass located and directly fetched DNR's own official implementing guidance — State Form 56490's "Commercial Film and Photography Application and Agreement Instructions" — resolving the citation/discrepancy flag left open in the original pass. DNR's guidance confirms drones are "generally prohibited on DNR properties to protect the privacy and safety of our guests and to protect the facilities and natural and cultural resources we conserve," but describes four specific exception categories, each still requiring advance permit-application review and an FAA license (three of four also require proof of insurance): (1) professional journalists covering natural/cultural-resource or agency stories; (2) university researchers under an appropriate DNR research permit; (3) documentary filmmakers producing a non-for-profit documentary in association with a news agency or nonprofit; and (4) state, regional, or county tourism agencies producing promotional material. This is more precise and complete than the three-category description found on secondary drone-law aggregator sites (which omitted the documentary-filmmaker category). **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Do not assume any of the four DNR exception categories applies to standard AEC survey, mapping, or inspection work — none of them cover commercial engineering, construction, or infrastructure-inspection UAS use. Treat any DNR-property launch or landing for AEC purposes as requiring a site-specific request to the property manager well in advance (DNR recommends 90 days for filming/photography permits). - **Agency Practitioner:** Contact the relevant DNR division directly based on property type: the Outreach Coordinator (317-233-3864) for state parks/reservoirs/recreation areas, the Assistant State Forester (317-232-4101) for state forests, or the Assistant Director for Public Lands (317-232-8059) for fish & wildlife areas and nature preserves. Submit the DNR Commercial Film and Photography Agreement and budget at least 90 days for review. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** DNR's discretionary exception practice is documented in agency guidance, not the rule itself, so treat it as agency policy subject to change rather than a codified right. Confirm current DNR practice directly before advising a client that any exception category applies to a specific AEC engagement. ### Indiana State Police — Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System Authority (IC 10-22) *Binding law | Current (effective July 1, 2026); federal trigger condition now satisfied — see below* **Objective Summary:** New IC Article 10-22, added by Senate Bill 227 (2026 Reg. Sess.), designates the Indiana State Police as the statewide coordinating agency for counter-UAS activities authorized under federal law. It authorizes the state police to seek federal authorization to acquire, deploy, and operate counter-UAS systems; to designate local law-enforcement "participating agencies"; to designate Indianapolis as a pilot-project location; and to designate "high-risk sites" including critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports, and large public/special-event-rated events. Counter-UAS systems must appear on the federal C-UAS Technology List. By its own terms, the article's substantive detection/mitigation authority applies only once a qualifying federal law is enacted and the Governor has published notice in the Indiana Register. **Update from this retrofit pass:** the federal-law half of that trigger has since been satisfied — DOJ and DHS published an interim final rule implementing the federal SAFER SKIES Act's counter-UAS authority for state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement and correctional agencies in the Federal Register on July 6, 2026 (effective July 1, 2026). Independent secondary reporting states Indiana's own state-law authority "became effective" March 4, 2026 in anticipation of this federal action. Direct confirmation that the Governor has published the required notice in the Indiana Register (the second half of the trigger) was not located in this pass. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** This article governs Indiana State Police and designated local law-enforcement counter-UAS authority, not private AEC operators — it does not restrict where or how an AEC firm may fly. At any designated "high-risk site" or in the Indianapolis pilot-project area, confirm with the site owner or event organizer whether counter-UAS detection or mitigation activity may be active before mobilizing, since a legitimate AEC flight could be misidentified as a threat, particularly now that the federal trigger condition has been satisfied. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** This is not a categorical purchasing ban, but it creates potential equipment-loss exposure near protected locations, now that the federal authorization trigger has been satisfied. Consider loss risk, insurance treatment, geofencing configuration, and replaceability when assigning aircraft to work in the affected environment. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Confirm current operational status directly with the Indiana State Police before assuming active counter-UAS detection or mitigation operations are underway at any specific Indiana site — the federal trigger is satisfied, but gubernatorial notice publication was not independently confirmed in this pass. ### Professional Licensing — Indiana Land Surveyors Statute (IC 25-21.5-1-7) *Binding law | MAJOR FINDING in this retrofit pass — a specific photogrammetry/remote-sensing supervision requirement* **Objective Summary:** Defines the "practice of surveying" broadly, and subsection (c) lists activities — including "the creation of maps and geo-referenced data bases representing authoritative locations for boundaries, fixed works, or topography, either by terrestrial surveying methods or by photogrammetric or GNSS locations" — that must be accomplished under the responsible charge of a professional surveyor unless specifically exempted under subsection (d). This retrofit pass fetched and read subsections (d) and (e) directly for the first time (the original pass located only the general framework via a secondary aggregator). Subsection (d) lists categories NOT included in the practice of surveying most relevant to AEC UAS work — general illustrative/educational maps, GIS transcription clearly not intended as authoritative, an organization's own internal facility-inventory maps/databases (with appropriate metadata and disclaimers), and natural-resource maps by foresters, geologists, soil scientists, or biologists. Separately, and previously unlocated, **subsection (e) provides that "the use of photogrammetric methods or similar remote sensing technology to perform any part of the practice of surveying... may be performed only under the direct control and supervision of a professional surveyor or professional photogrammetrist who maintain[s] a current title of 'Certified Photogrammetrist' from a national scientific organization"** — a specific supervision requirement directly applicable to UAS-derived photogrammetric survey products, independent of the subsection (c)/(d) authoritative-location analysis. No standalone Indiana Professional Licensing Agency or State Board of Registration for Professional Surveyors rule, advisory opinion, or FAQ specifically addressing UAS platforms (as distinct from photogrammetric methods generally) was located. **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Classify each UAS-derived deliverable against subsections (c) through (e), not just a general competency framework. Authoritative boundary/fixed-works/topographic products must be produced under the responsible charge of a licensed PLS, OR under the direct control and supervision of a professional surveyor or a nationally certified photogrammetrist per subsection (e) — a distinct, separately-applicable requirement for photogrammetric/remote-sensing methods. General-purpose, non-authoritative maps or internal inventory databases with appropriate metadata and disclaimers (subsection (d)) may fall outside licensed practice, but document that classification decision. - **Agency Practitioner:** Before relying on an unlicensed or exempt delivery path, give the Board a written description of the proposed UAS-derived product and confirm both whether it falls within subsection (c)/(d)'s authoritative-location analysis AND whether subsection (e)'s photogrammetrist-supervision requirement is separately satisfied. Retain the board's response with the project quality plan. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Subsection (e)'s supervision requirement applies specifically to photogrammetric and remote-sensing methods — squarely covering most UAS-derived mapping products — independent of whether the deliverable also falls within subsection (c)'s authoritative-location categories. Confirm which licensed or certified individual is exercising the required supervision for any UAS photogrammetry deliverable, and document that chain, before delivery. ### Governor's Office — Executive Order 25-73, Indiana Initiative for Drone Dominance Task Force *Official agency policy | Task force established; statutory strategic-plan deadline of July 31, 2026 has passed* **Objective Summary:** Governor Mike Braun signed Executive Order 25-73 (on or about October 29-30, 2025), establishing the "Indiana Initiative for Drone Dominance Task Force," a multi-agency, university, and industry body directed to develop a strategic plan supporting federal "American drone dominance" policy, drawing on assets such as NSWC Crane, Camp Atterbury, and Muscatatuck Urban Training Center. Stated priorities include a cross-sector aerial test corridor, expanding public-safety UAS applications at major events, strengthening Indiana's drone manufacturing supply chain, and exploring counter-UAS infrastructure. The task force owed its strategic plan and recommendations to the Governor by July 31, 2026. Indiana was separately designated a national drone test site in January 2026, consistent with the task force's test-corridor priority. A search in this retrofit pass, conducted one week after the statutory deadline, did not locate a published version of the completed strategic plan; its status should be confirmed directly with the Governor's office. This record previously combined this affirmative finding with several negative-finding categories (no AG opinion, no court decision, no general state-agency UAS procurement restriction beyond IC 10-22, no local-ordinance preemption statute); those categories have been moved to the checklist in this retrofit pass per `Agent_Instructions.v6.md` §5.2, since the prior combined record's own `source_type` field said "not included in the final source register." **Practical Interpretation** - **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** This order does not itself impose an operator-facing requirement, but AEC firms with drone-manufacturing, testing, or supply-chain interests should monitor the task force's strategic plan (status not yet confirmed as published) for emerging state incentive programs or test-corridor access opportunities. - **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process. - **UAS Procurement Expert:** No current state equipment restriction or incentive program is established by this order alone. Monitor the task force's strategic plan for any resulting state-level manufacturing, procurement, or supply-chain program relevant to fleet decisions. - **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Treat this as a policy-development and coordination vehicle, not a source of operator-facing legal obligations. Confirm the task force's current status and any resulting legislative or administrative action directly with the Governor's office. ## 4. Non-Regulatory Context A Section 4.7 news-aggregator pass (required closing step of this retrofit, standardizing this state's prior inline news list onto the project's now-established `*_UAS_News.yaml` + inline-anchor workflow) retained one genuine, substantive match: the Indiana Capital Chronicle's April 27, 2026 in-depth feature "Rural Hoosiers lean on the law to fight drones," anchored inline under IN-003 above. It covers the specific incidents and testimony (an Adams County drone swarm near poultry barns amid avian-flu fears, a homeowner followed by a drone near Shelbyville) that drove the 2026 "remote aerial harassment" expansion to livestock, crops, and farm operations, and separately reports the sentencing outcome (60 days probation, a one-year hunting/fishing license revocation, and a pretrial-diversion agreement for a co-defendant) in Indiana's first prosecution under the UAV-aided-hunting statute (IC 14-22-6-16, IN-006). See `IN_UAS_News.yaml` for the full citation. The Pettit hunting-prosecution details and the Executive Order 25-73 task-force announcement previously appeared here as separate inline items; both are now folded directly into their respective register records' own objective content (IN-006 and the rewritten IN-010) rather than duplicated as separate news items, consistent with this project's standing redundancy-avoidance rule for news that describes the same underlying development as an already-updated record. ## 5. Unresolved Operational Questions - **IC 35-45-10-6 amended text:** RECONFIRMED UNRESOLVED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS. The exact codified text of the July 1, 2026 "remote aerial harassment" expansion to livestock, crops, and farm operations (H.E.A. 1249/P.L.158-2026) still could not be verified against a primary codification mirror as of August 7, 2026 (more than five weeks post-effective-date, across two independent research passes); confirm current statutory language directly with the Indiana General Assembly before relying on it for agricultural or rural-corridor flight planning. - **312 IAC 8-2-8(i) exception practice:** RESOLVED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS. DNR's own official State Form 56490 guidance was located and confirms four specific exception categories (journalists, university researchers, documentary filmmakers, tourism agencies), each requiring advance permit review; see IN-007 above. - **IC 10-22 (counter-UAS) operative status:** PARTIALLY RESOLVED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS. The federal-law half of the operative trigger has been satisfied (DOJ/DHS SAFER SKIES Act interim final rule, effective July 1, 2026); direct confirmation of the Governor's Indiana Register notice publication was not located. Confirm current status directly with the Indiana State Police before assuming active counter-UAS operations near any specific Indiana site. - **State preemption of local ordinances:** No statewide preemption statute was located, and Fort Wayne (City Ordinance Sec. 96.30) and Carmel (City Ordinance Sec. 6-69) maintain their own local drone ordinances. Local ordinances are out of scope for this Phase 1, state-level pass, but AEC firms should check locally-adopted rules for any Indiana project site given the apparent absence of statewide preemption. - **Critical-infrastructure trespass fit:** Indiana's general critical-infrastructure-facility trespass statute (IC 35-46-10-2) does not on its face reference UAS or airspace, and its application to drone overflight (versus physical entry onto real property) is unresolved; it was excluded from the source register on that basis but may warrant monitoring for future amendment or judicial construction. - **IC 25-21.5-1-7 subsection (e) certified-photogrammetrist requirement:** RESOLVED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS as to its existence and text; whether a specific UAS-derived deliverable satisfies subsection (e)'s supervision requirement remains fact-specific and was not resolved against current Indiana Professional Licensing Agency/Board guidance for any particular deliverable type. ## 6. Moderate for the July 2026 livestock/crops/farm-operations amendment (still not reflected in a primary codification mirror as of this retrofit's research date, reconfirmed) | | IC 35-44.1-3-5 / -3-6 (correctional-facility UAV contraband trafficking) | High — verified directly against Justia's Indiana Code mirror | | IC 35-44.1-4-10 (public safety remote aerial interference) | High — verified directly against Justia's Indiana Code mirror | | IC 14-22-6-16 (UAV-aided-hunting restriction) | High — verified directly against Justia's Indiana Code mirror; enforcement corroborated by 2026 prosecution reporting | | 312 IAC 8-2-8(i) (DNR property landing/launch prohibition) | High — rule text confirmed directly via Cornell LII; DNR's own official State Form 56490 guidance directly confirmed and resolved the prior exception-category discrepancy in this retrofit pass | | IC 10-22 (counter-UAS statewide coordination authority) | High that the article was enacted and that the federal trigger is now satisfied; Moderate on full current operative status (gubernatorial notice publication not independently confirmed) | | IC 25-21.5-1-7 (professional land surveying framework, including the subsection (e) photogrammetrist-supervision requirement) | High — full current text of subsections (a) through (f) fetched and read directly against Justia's codification in this retrofit pass, replacing a secondary-aggregator-only citation | | Executive Order 25-73 (Indiana Initiative for Drone Dominance Task Force) | Moderate — corroborated by multiple independent secondary sources after the primary PDF proved non-machine-readable in two research passes | | No AG opinion / court decision / general state-agency procurement restriction / local preemption statute located | Low — negative research findings, not a comprehensive search; records.summary: IC 35-45-4-5(g) makes it remote aerial voyeurism for a person, with intent to peep, to operate a UAV so that it enters the airspace above or surrounding another person's occupied dwelling to capture images, photographs, video, or audio of that person while inside the dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area, without consent. Subsection (h) elevates the offense to a Level 6 felony for a repeat offense or if the material is published, posted online, or transmitted to another person. This is a subsection within Indiana's broader voyeurism statute (Sec. 5), distinct from the separate remote aerial harassment offense at IC 35-45-10-6 (IN-003).
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not operate a UAV with intent to peep or capture images of a person inside an occupied dwelling or on adjoining land not visible from a public area, without consent -- this is a felony-eligible offense distinct from the broader voyeurism statute. Routine AEC survey, inspection, and mapping photography is not the conduct this subsection targets, but frame flight paths and camera angles to avoid incidental capture into private dwelling interiors, and never publish, post, or transmit any such incidental capture given subsection (h)'s felony-elevation trigger for publication.

records.regulated_activity: Pre-amendment: operating a UAV in a manner intended to subject another person to harassment. Per multiple news reports describing H.E.A. 1249 (P.L.158-2026, eff. 7-1-2026): also operating a UAV over another person's property with intent to harass or disturb livestock, damage crops, or interfere with farm/agricultural operations
records.requirement_type: Prohibition (Class A misdemeanor; Level 6 felony for a prior unrelated conviction)
records.summary: As currently codified in the primary-source mirrors reviewed, IC 35-45-10-6 makes it remote aerial harassment, a Class A misdemeanor (Level 6 felony on repeat offense), to operate a UAV in a manner intended to subject another person to harassment. Multiple independent news outlets (Indiana Capital Chronicle, Indiana Public Radio/WFIU, Hoosier Ag Today) report that House Enrolled Act 1249 (P.L.158-2026), signed by the Governor in March 2026 and effective July 1, 2026, expanded this statute so that operating a drone over another's property with intent to harass or disturb livestock, damage crops, or interfere with agricultural operations is also a Class A misdemeanor, following farmer complaints of unauthorized drone activity over poultry barns amid avian-flu concerns in northeastern Indiana.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not operate a UAV in a manner intended to harass another person, or -- once the July 1, 2026 livestock/crops/farm-operations amendment takes effect in the codified text -- to harass or disturb livestock, damage crops, or interfere with farm operations. Obtain the landowner's documented permission before any agricultural, corridor, or rural-property flight, and brief crews that intent to harass (not merely proximity to livestock or crops) is the operative element, consistent with the law's stated goal of preserving legitimate agricultural drone uses such as crop monitoring and chemical application.

news.headline: Rural Hoosiers lean on the law to fight drones
news.relevance_note: Directly on-topic for IN-003's remote aerial harassment statute and its 2026 expansion to livestock, crops, and farm operations: reports the specific incidents and testimony that drove the amendment, including an Adams County cluster of eight-plus drones near poultry barns amid avian-flu fears (with Indiana Department of Homeland Security and FBI/FAA involvement), a Jay County farmer's testimony before the legislature, and a Shelbyville-area resident's account of a drone hovering 50-60 feet from her home. Also reports the sentencing outcome (60 days probation, a one-year hunting/fishing license revocation, and a pretrial-diversion agreement for a co-defendant) in Indiana's first prosecution under the separate UAV-aided-hunting statute (IC 14-22-6-16, IN-006) -- that prosecution itself is already folded into IN-006's own objective content and is not treated as a second, redundant news item here.

records.citation: IC 35-44.1-3-5 and IC 35-44.1-3-6 (both amended by P.L.22-2024, part of Senate Enrolled Act 182, signed 2024-03-11)
records.regulated_activity: Delivering, carrying, or receiving contraband or another article to or from an inmate of a penal/juvenile facility, or delivering/placing contraband for an inmate being transported outside a facility, including by means of an unmanned aerial vehicle, without the facility head's prior authorization
records.requirement_type: Prohibition (Class A misdemeanor; Level 5 felony if the article is a controlled substance, chemical intoxicant, deadly weapon, or wireless device; Level 6 or Level 5 felony under Sec. 6 depending on contraband type)
records.permit_or_approval_required: N/A (facility head's prior authorization is the only avoidance mechanism)
records.summary: IC 35-44.1-3-5 makes it trafficking with an inmate, a Class A misdemeanor (Level 5 felony for certain contraband), to deliver, carry, or receive an article to or from an inmate or juvenile-facility resident without the facility head's prior authorization, expressly including delivery, carrying, or receipt 'through the use of an unmanned aerial vehicle.' IC 35-44.1-3-6 creates a parallel offense, trafficking with an inmate outside a facility, for delivering or placing contraband where an inmate being transported outside a facility could obtain it, likewise expressly including delivery or placement by UAV. Both sections were amended in 2024 (P.L.22-2024) as part of Senate Enrolled Act 182, enacted after the Indiana Department of Correction reported more than 30 drone sightings and over a dozen confirmed drone-delivered contraband drops at state correctional facilities in 2023.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Secure the facility head's prior written authorization before any UAV flight at or near a correctional or juvenile facility, regardless of the flight's purpose -- the statute's prior-authorization requirement is the only avoidance mechanism and applies to any person, not just inmates or visitors. Confirm the facility's specific point of contact, required lead time, and any site-specific conditions well before mobilization.
records.practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact the protected facility's owner, operator, administrator, commander, or other official identified by the authority before mobilization and ask whether the proposed AEC mission qualifies for written approval or an employment/contractor exception. Provide the site, purpose, dates, flight area, crew and aircraft details the facility requests, and retain the signed authorization and security conditions; do not assume ordinary site access or a client work order is sufficient.

records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Make the required approval and compliance with its conditions a documented mobilization gate. Allocate responsibility for applications and schedule impacts in the contract, and obtain counsel if the project's facts do not fit the stated authorization pathway.

records.uas_topic: UAV-aided-hunting restriction (wildlife/hunting), with agricultural-monitoring and post-harvest-recovery exceptions
records.regulated_party: Hunters and the general public (exceptions for DNR and its designees, government agents, educational/research institutions, veterinary care, and agricultural/nuisance-animal monitoring)
records.regulated_activity: Using a UAV to search for, scout, locate, or detect a wild animal to which a hunting season applies, as an aid to taking that animal, during the period beginning 14 days before the season and running through its last legal hunting hour
records.requirement_type: Prohibition during the defined season window; UAV-aided recovery of an already-legally-taken animal (including with infrared) is expressly permitted, but does not authorize entering another's property without permission
records.summary: IC 14-22-6-16(c) prohibits knowingly using a UAV to search for, scout, locate, or detect a wild animal covered by a hunting season, as an aid to taking it, during a window beginning 14 days before that season and ending at the close of legal hunting hours on the season's last day. Subsection (d) permits using a UAV with infrared capability to locate and recover an already-legally-taken animal, but does not authorize entering another person's property without the landowner's permission. Subsection (a) exempts the department and its designees, government-agency employees/agents performing official duties, educational/research institution personnel for bona fide purposes, UAV use to assist or provide veterinary care to a specific wild animal, and UAV use to monitor agricultural production or nuisance wild animals.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental and mapping flights to avoid conduct that could be characterized as locating, pursuing, disturbing, or harassing wildlife. Coordinate mission timing and stand-off distances with the land manager when project work overlaps sensitive habitat or hunting activity.

records.jurisdiction_name: Indiana (DNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property statewide, including state parks, state forests, state recreation areas, nature preserves, fish and wildlife areas, and reservoir properties)
records.issuing_authority: Indiana Natural Resources Commission / Indiana Department of Natural Resources
records.source_title: Vehicles, Trails, Boats, and Aircraft -- Airborne-Device Prohibition on DNR Property
records.citation: 312 IAC 8-2-8(i) (Natural Resources Commission rule; most recently amended/readopted per filing 1/25/2024, eff. 20240221-IR-312230538FRA)
records.effective_date: Unknown original adoption date (rule filed Oct. 28, 1998, eff. Jan. 1, 1999); most recently amended effective per Feb. 2024 filing
records.uas_topic: State park/public land UAV landing and launch prohibition
records.regulated_party: Any person, including AEC/commercial UAS operators
records.regulated_activity: Landing, taxiing, taking off, parking, or mooring an unmanned motor-driven airborne device (or an airborne human transportation device) on DNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property
records.requirement_type: Prohibition except at a site designated by the Department for that purpose; DNR's own published guidance separately describes a discretionary launch/film licensing practice administered by DNR or a specific DNR division
records.permit_or_approval_required: Yes -- per DNR's own published guidance, a discretionary license from DNR or the relevant DNR division, plus an FAA license and proof of insurance, may be required outside a designated site; contact the property manager
records.summary: 312 IAC 8-2-8(i) prohibits a person from landing, taxiing, taking off, parking, or mooring an unmanned motor-driven airborne device, or an airborne human transportation device, on DNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property, except at a site the Department has designated for that purpose. The rule's own text contains no enumerated exceptions. This retrofit pass located and directly fetched DNR's own official implementing guidance -- State Form 56490's 'Commercial Film and Photography Application and Agreement Instructions' (in.gov/dnr) -- which resolves the citation discrepancy flagged in the original pass. DNR's own guidance confirms drones are 'generally prohibited on DNR properties to protect the privacy and safety of our guests and to protect the facilities and natural and cultural resources we conserve,' but describes four specific exception categories, each still requiring advance permit-application review, providing a copy of the drone operator's FAA license, and (for three of the four) proof of insurance: (1) professional journalists working on pieces informing the public about natural/cultural resources or agency activities (a commercial filming application is not typically required); (2) university researchers with an appropriate DNR research permit, where the drone use is warranted by the project design; (3) documentary filmmakers producing a non-for-profit documentary about DNR-managed resources, staff, or facilities, in association with a news agency or nonprofit (a commercial filming application is required); and (4) state, regional, or county tourism agencies or their partners producing promotional film, video, or still photography (a commercial filming application is required). This is a more precise and complete picture than either the rule's own bare text or the secondary drone-law aggregator sites' abbreviated three-category description (which omitted the documentary-filmmaker category and did not distinguish which categories require a full commercial filming application).
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not assume any of the four DNR exception categories applies to standard AEC survey, mapping, or inspection work -- none of them cover commercial engineering, construction, or infrastructure-inspection UAS use. Treat any DNR-property launch or landing for AEC purposes as requiring a site-specific request to the property manager well in advance (DNR recommends 90 days for filming/photography permits), since AEC work does not fit any of the four enumerated categories and would need to be evaluated case-by-case.
records.practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact the relevant DNR division directly based on property type: the Outreach Coordinator (317-233-3864) for state parks, reservoirs, state recreation areas, and off-road riding areas; the Assistant State Forester (317-232-4101) for state forests; or the Assistant Director for Public Lands (317-232-8059) for fish & wildlife areas and dedicated nature preserves. Submit the DNR Commercial Film and Photography Agreement, provide the drone operator's FAA license and proof of insurance where the request falls within one of the four recognized exception categories, and budget at least 90 days for review given DNR's own stated processing expectations.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: The rule's bare text (312 IAC 8-2-8(i)) is an unqualified prohibition with no textual exceptions; DNR's discretionary exception practice is documented in agency guidance (State Form 56490 instructions), not the rule itself, so it should be treated as agency policy subject to change rather than a codified right. Confirm current DNR practice directly before advising a client that any exception category applies to a specific AEC engagement.
records.verification_status: Full current rule text (subsection (i)) verified directly against Cornell LII's mirror of 312 IAC 8-2-8 in the original pass. records.issuing_authority: Indiana General Assembly / Indiana State Police
records.citation: IC 10-22 (new article added by Senate Bill 227, 2026 Reg. Sess.; ceremonially signed by Governor Braun April 23, 2026; eff. 2026-07-01)
records.status: Current / in force (effective date passed; the federal trigger has since been satisfied -- see notes)
records.uas_topic: Counter-UAS (detection/mitigation) statewide coordination; critical-infrastructure/correctional-facility/airport 'high-risk site' designation; procurement restricted to the federal C-UAS Technology List
records.regulated_party: Indiana State Police (statewide coordinating agency); designated local law-enforcement 'participating agencies'
records.regulated_activity: State police authority to apply for federal counter-UAS authorization, coordinate detection/tracking/identification/mitigation activity by trained personnel, designate 'high-risk sites' (large public events, federally-rated special events, critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports) and a pilot-project location (Indianapolis), and restrict counter-UAS procurement to systems on the federal C-UAS Technology List
records.requirement_type: Authorizing/coordinating framework -- by its own terms (Article 22, Ch. 1), the article's substantive counter-UAS authority applies only once a triggering federal law is enacted and the Governor publishes notice in the Indiana Register
records.permit_or_approval_required: N/A (governs state agency authority, not private-operator permitting)
records.summary: New IC Article 10-22, added by Senate Bill 227 (2026 Reg. Sess.), designates the Indiana State Police as the statewide coordinating agency for counter-UAS activities authorized under federal law. It authorizes the state police to seek federal authorization to acquire, deploy, and operate counter-UAS systems; to designate local law-enforcement 'participating agencies' meeting federal training/readiness requirements; to designate Indianapolis as a pilot-project location given its concentration of high-risk sites; and to designate 'high-risk sites' including critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports, and large public/special-event-rated events. Counter-UAS systems must appear on the federal C-UAS Technology List. By its own terms (Chapter 1), the article applies only once a federal law authorizing state/local detection, tracking, identification, or mitigation of UAS is enacted and the Governor has published notice of that authorization in the Indiana Register; mitigation activity is barred absent express federal authorization.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This article governs Indiana State Police and designated local law-enforcement counter-UAS authority, not private AEC operators -- it does not restrict where or how an AEC firm may fly. The practical relevance is airspace/operational awareness: at any of the article's designated 'high-risk sites' (critical infrastructure, correctional facilities, airports, large public/special-rated events) or in the Indianapolis pilot-project area, confirm with the site owner or event organizer whether counter-UAS detection or mitigation activity may be active before mobilizing, since a legitimate AEC flight could be misidentified as a threat.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: This equipment restriction governs agency counter-UAS systems, not ordinary AEC aircraft or payloads. Do not treat it as a fleet-eligibility rule unless the contract requires the firm to furnish detection or mitigation technology.
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Make the required approval and compliance with its conditions a documented mobilization gate. Allocate responsibility for applications and schedule impacts in the contract, and obtain counsel if the project's facts do not fit the stated authorization pathway.
records.verification_status: Full bill text (as reported favorably out of committee, Jan. 21, 2026, reflecting the enacted new-article structure) verified directly against an official Indiana General Assembly legislative document; the bill's passage and the Governor's April 23, 2026 ceremonial signing are corroborated by an Indiana House Republicans caucus press release. The final codified IC 10-22 text was not independently re-verified against a post-enactment primary codification mirror as of the date accessed.
records.notes: UPDATED IN THIS RETROFIT PASS: the article's federal-law trigger condition has been satisfied since the original research pass. DOJ and DHS published an interim final rule implementing the federal SAFER SKIES Act's Counter-UAS Authority for State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Law Enforcement and Correctional Agencies in the Federal Register on July 6, 2026 (effective July 1, 2026), establishing the detection/warning and mitigation certification framework this Indiana article's own trigger provision (Chapter 1) requires. Independent secondary reporting states Indiana's own state-law authority 'became effective' March 4, 2026 in anticipation of this federal action. However, direct confirmation that the Governor has published the required notice in the Indiana Register (the second half of the state-law trigger) was not located in this pass -- confirm current operational status directly with the Indiana State Police before assuming active counter-UAS detection or mitigation operations are underway at any specific Indiana site.

records.issuing_authority: Indiana Professional Licensing Agency / Indiana State Board of Registration for Professional Surveyors
records.source_title: 'Practice of Surveying' -- General Definition, Specific Non-Surveying Exemptions (Subsection (d)), and Photogrammetry/Remote-Sensing Supervision Requirement (Subsection (e))
records.citation: IC 25-21.5-1-7 (Indiana Land Surveyors licensing statute, Definitions)
records.effective_date: Unknown original enactment date; definitions section subsequently amended
records.binding_level: Binding (general licensing framework only -- no UAS-specific rule or guidance identified)
records.uas_topic: General professional-licensing competency for photogrammetric/GNSS survey methods (no UAS-specific rule or guidance located)
records.regulated_party: Licensed Professional Surveyors; persons performing survey-grade measurement of boundaries, fixed works, or topography
records.regulated_activity: Practicing land surveying -- including photogrammetric- or GNSS-based determination of boundaries, fixed works, or topography intended to be authoritative -- without licensure or outside an applicable statutory exemption
records.requirement_type: Licensure requirement for work performed 'under the responsible charge' of a professional surveyor, subject to a statutory exemption pathway (subsection (d)) for defined circumstances
records.permit_or_approval_required: License (PLS) generally required for boundary-related or authoritative topographic surveying work; a subsection (d) exemption may remove certain UAS-derived deliverables from the licensure requirement if its conditions are met
records.summary: IC 25-21.5-1-7 defines the 'practice of surveying' broadly to include making geometric measurements of, and gathering information about, the physical or legal features of the earth or the space above it, and developing that information into survey products. Subsection (c) lists activities -- including 'the creation of maps and geo-referenced data bases representing authoritative locations for boundaries, fixed works, or topography, either by terrestrial surveying methods or by photogrammetric or GNSS locations' -- that must be accomplished under the responsible charge of a professional surveyor unless specifically exempted under subsection (d). This retrofit pass fetched and read subsections (d) and (e) directly against Justia's codification for the first time (the original pass located only the general framework via a secondary aggregator, LawServer). Subsection (d) lists nine specific categories NOT included in the practice of surveying, most relevant to AEC UAS work: general maps prepared as guides or illustrative/educational tools (not clearly the same as authoritative boundary work); transcription of previously geo-referenced data into a GIS where the data are 'clearly not intended to indicate the authoritative location of property boundaries, the precise definition of the shape or contour of the earth, and the precise location of fixed works'; inventory maps/databases of an organization's own physical features/facilities/infrastructure, provided the data carry appropriate metadata (accuracy, compilation method, source, date) and disclaimers that they are not survey products; and maps/data depicting natural resources prepared by foresters, geologists, soil scientists, biologists, or similarly qualified non-surveyor professionals. Separately, and previously unlocated in the original pass, subsection (e) provides that 'the use of photogrammetric methods or similar remote sensing technology to perform any part of the practice of surveying... may be performed only under the direct control and supervision of a professional surveyor or professional photogrammetrist who maintain[s] a current title of "Certified Photogrammetrist" from a national scientific organization having a process for certifying photogrammetrists' -- a specific, previously unflagged supervision requirement directly applicable to UAS-derived photogrammetric survey products. No standalone Indiana Professional Licensing Agency or State Board of Registration for Professional Surveyors rule, advisory opinion, or FAQ specifically addressing UAS platforms (as distinct from photogrammetric methods generally) was located during this research pass.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Classify each UAS-derived deliverable against subsections (c) through (e) before mobilization, not just the general competency framework. If the product is intended to establish an authoritative boundary, fixed-works, or topographic location (orthomosaics, geo-referenced surface models, boundary-adjacent products), it must be produced under the responsible charge of a licensed PLS, OR under the direct control and supervision of a professional surveyor or a nationally certified photogrammetrist per subsection (e) -- a distinct, separately-applicable supervision requirement for photogrammetric/remote-sensing methods. If the product is a general-purpose, non-authoritative map or an internal facility-inventory database with appropriate metadata and disclaimers (subsection (d)), it may fall outside licensed practice, but document that classification decision and its basis in the project file.
records.practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Before relying on an unlicensed or exempt delivery path, give Indiana Professional Licensing Agency / Indiana State Board of Registration for Professional Surveyors a written description of the proposed UAS-derived product, its stated accuracy, and whether it will establish or certify boundaries, elevations, or authoritative locations -- and separately confirm whether subsection (e)'s photogrammetrist-supervision requirement is satisfied by the proposed production workflow, since it applies independently of the subsection (c)/(d) authoritative-location analysis. Retain the board's response with the project quality plan.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is now a materially more precise finding than a general framework-only citation: subsection (e)'s photogrammetrist/professional-surveyor supervision requirement applies specifically to photogrammetric and remote-sensing methods (squarely covering most UAS-derived mapping products) independent of whether the specific deliverable also falls within subsection (c)'s authoritative-location categories. Confirm which licensed or certified individual is exercising the required supervision for any UAS photogrammetry deliverable, and document that chain, before delivery.

records.citation: Executive Order 25-73 (Governor Mike Braun, signed on or about 2025-10-29/30)
records.status: Current / in force (task force established; statutory strategic-plan deadline of 2026-07-31 has passed -- see notes)

records.uas_topic: State drone-industry strategic planning and interagency coordination
records.summary: Governor Mike Braun signed Executive Order 25-73 (on or about October 29-30, 2025), establishing the 'Indiana Initiative for Drone Dominance Task Force,' a multi-agency, university, and industry body directed to develop a strategic plan supporting federal 'American drone dominance' policy, drawing on assets such as NSWC Crane, Camp Atterbury, and Muscatatuck Urban Training Center. Stated priorities include a cross-sector aerial test corridor connecting these sites, expanding public-safety UAS applications at major events, strengthening Indiana's drone manufacturing supply chain (including smaller and emerging firms), and exploring counter-UAS detection/tracking/neutralization infrastructure. The task force owed its strategic plan and recommendations to the Governor by July 31, 2026. In a related development, Indiana was designated a national drone test site in January 2026 (Indiana Capital Chronicle, WFYI, WBIW), consistent with the task force's aerial-test-corridor priority. A search in this retrofit pass (conducted one week after the July 31, 2026 statutory deadline) did not locate a published version of the task force's completed strategic plan; its current status should be confirmed directly with the Governor's office or the Indiana Economic Development Corporation.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This order does not itself impose an operator-facing requirement, but AEC firms with drone-manufacturing, testing, or supply-chain interests should monitor the task force's strategic plan (due July 31, 2026, status not yet confirmed as published) for emerging state incentive programs, test-corridor access opportunities, or related state initiatives.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: No current state equipment restriction or incentive program is established by this order alone. Monitor the task force's strategic plan for any resulting state-level manufacturing, procurement, or supply-chain program relevant to fleet decisions.
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat this as a policy-development and coordination vehicle, not a source of operator-facing legal obligations. Confirm the task force's current status and any resulting legislative or administrative action directly with the Governor's office before advising a client on state drone-industry incentives.
records.verification_status: The Executive Order 25-73 PDF (in.gov/gov/files/EO-Drone.pdf) was located again in this retrofit pass but again returned as an empty/non-machine-readable file; its existence, number, date, and substantive content continue to be corroborated via multiple independent secondary sources (Indiana Capital Chronicle, WFYI, WBIW, a U.S. Senator's press release, and Indiana public-radio coverage), consistent with the original pass. A direct search for the task force's July 31, 2026 statutory-deadline strategic plan did not locate a published version as of this retrofit's research date.
